sum: По данным Evertiq, 10 ноября компания Ericsson запустила интегрированную систему обнаружения и связи, которая использует мобильные сети для обнаружения и отслеживания дронов, включая устройства, не подключенные к сети.

Система использует радиостанции 5G с сенсорными возможностями для анализа отраженных сигналов на нескольких сетевых сайтах. Эрикссон утверждает, что распределенный подход может повысить точность позиционирования и отслеживания в зоне покрытия при использовании уже развернутой инфраструктуры для мобильной связи.

Продукт предназначен для приложений безопасности и критической инфраструктуры, включая обнаружение небольших дронов, используемых для незаконного наблюдения, саботажа или ведения боевых действий. Ericsson представляет систему как дополнение к радару и другим датчикам, а не как замену.

Согласно отчету, полевые испытания позволили обнаружить и отследить микродроны на расстоянии нескольких километров с помощью трехмерного позиционирования. В испытаниях приняли участие AT&T в Арлингтоне, штат Техас, и Erillisverkot в Хельсинки. В Польше Ericsson, оператор Play и Asseco объединили эту технологию с акустической системой обнаружения дронов.

Ожидается, что мелкомасштабные коммерческие пилотные проекты, предназначенные только для зондирования, начнутся в 2027 году, а более широкое развертывание запланировано на 2028 год. Коммуникационный элемент системы будет развиваться дальше по мере продвижения Ericsson к возможностям 6G.

Для инвесторов запуск расширяет потенциальные возможности Ericsson, выходя за рамки традиционных подключений и управления сетью. Коммерческой проверкой станет то, приведут ли пилотные проекты к постоянному получению доходов от оборудования, программного обеспечения и услуг.

sum: Ericsson and Singtel announced a five-year strategic partnership on October 20, 2026, to advance Singapore's 5G capabilities and accelerate AI-native applications. The companies said the agreement will support more reliable and intelligent connectivity for businesses and consumers, according to Ericsson.

The roadmap extends cooperation announced in March 2026 and focuses on scaling 5G Advanced and AI-powered network capabilities across industries. Planned applications include autonomous vehicles, industrial robotics, smart manufacturing and intelligent logistics, where low latency, dedicated capacity and predictable performance are important.

Singtel and Ericsson also intend to widen the commercial use of network slicing and programmable connectivity. The companies will explore potential deployments at Changi Airport Terminal 5, Bulim Square and upcoming JTC developments, with possible uses including autonomous mobility, intelligent inspection, remote monitoring and real-time video analytics.

The partners plan to use artificial intelligence and machine learning to forecast traffic, optimise network resources and identify potential performance issues earlier. Ericsson said a live-network trial of AI-powered radio access capabilities improved throughput by 19 percent, highlighting the technical potential of the approach.

The agreement builds on Singtel's nationwide 5G standalone network and earlier work on network slicing. Ericsson said the partners also introduced network enhancements supporting peak uplink speeds of up to 250 Mbps on compatible newer devices. Singtel CEO Ng Tian Chong said the priority is to make advanced capabilities more widely accessible and commercially viable while strengthening network reliability, security and performance.

The partnership creates a longer runway for Ericsson's network modernization and software activities, but it does not disclose a contract value or an earnings target. For investors, the key question is whether planned deployments develop into recurring customer revenue rather than remaining a technology roadmap.

sum: Ericsson is extending its 5G growth narrative into defense, emergency response and drone detection after announcements in Sweden on November 5 and the launch of its ISAC system on November 2. The company says the applications could broaden the use of existing mobile-network infrastructure, but commercial revenue remains a future opportunity.

In an Ericsson newsroom update published on November 5, the Swedish Armed Forces said they plan to use 5G for military capabilities and communications. The network uses nationwide coverage supplied through Telia, where Ericsson is the infrastructure vendor, and can extend coverage to military bases, temporary field deployments and emergency airbases. It can also support equipment on amphibious craft, frigates and transport aircraft.

Ericsson said the capability is intended to complement existing military communication systems. The announcement does not specify a contract value, deployment volume or direct revenue contribution. Ericsson's newsroom update also linked the initiative to wider European emergency-communications plans.

Ericsson's Integrated Sensing and Communication system adds sensing capabilities to 5G networks. The system combines sensing-capable radios, edge computing, artificial intelligence and signal processing to detect and track moving objects, including drones that are not connected to the network. Ericsson presents the technology as a complement to radar and other sensors.

Selected small-scale, sensing-only commercial pilots are expected to begin in 2027, followed by broader sensing deployments from 2028. Ericsson's press release said the system had detected and tracked micro drones in validated tests over kilometer-scale distances.

sum: Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson (publ), together with its subsidiaries, provides mobile connectivity solutions to communications service providers, enterprises, and the public sector in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Northeast Asia, Southeast Asia, Oceania, and India. It operates through Networks; Cloud Software and Services; Enterprise; and Other segments. The Networks segment offers hardware, software, and service offerings for intelligent, reliable and flexible 5G networks. This segment also provides energy-efficient RAN with an AI-native software architecture deployable on Ericsson silicon and third-party CPUs/GPUs; transport networks; and active/ passive antennas, as well as deployment and lifecycle management services. The Cloud Software and Services segment provides core networks, network management, business and operations support systems, and network operations delivered as managed services, including secure data and voice connectivity, service monetization and orchestration tools, and network management services. The Enterprise segment offers intelligent networking and advanced communications software solutions comprising global communications platform, wireless wide area networks (WWAN), and private 5G networks. The Other segment includes RedBee Media that prepares and distributes live and on-demand video services for broadcasters, sports leagues, and communications service providers. The company has a strategic collaboration with T-Mobile US, Inc for the development of AI-native Scheduler with Link Adaptation software. The company was formerly known as Allmanna Telefon AB LM Ericsson and changed its name to Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson (publ) in January 1926. Telefonaktiebolaget LM Ericsson (publ) was founded in 1876 and is headquartered in Stockholm, Sweden.

Ericsson stock adds drone-detection growth angle with ISAC launch
sum: Ericsson introduced its Ericsson ISAC System on November 2, 2026, opening a new application for mobile-network infrastructure. The system adds sensing capabilities to 5G networks so operators can detect and track moving objects such as drones, including objects that are not connected to the network, according to an Ericsson press release.

The company is targeting defense, public safety and critical infrastructure operators. Ericsson said commercial introduction will begin with selected small-scale, sensing-only pilots in 2027. Broader sensing deployments are expected from 2028, while the integrated communications capability is planned to develop as the technology moves toward 6G.

The system analyzes reflections from radio signals and operates as a multi-static network. Transmission and reception are distributed across geographically separate mobile sites, allowing the system to view objects from multiple angles and maintain tracks across a coverage area.

Ericsson said the system uses parts of existing 5G infrastructure, including towers, backhaul and spectrum. It combines sensing-capable radios with edge computing, artificial intelligence and signal processing. The company says this approach can provide tracking data and AI-based classification through standardized interfaces with security and command systems.

Validated tests detected and tracked micro drones at kilometer-scale distances with precise 3D positioning. Ericsson cautioned that performance depends on the target, its flight profile, sensing geometry, terrain, surrounding environment and system configuration. The company presents the technology as a complement to radar and other sensors rather than a replacement.

Ericsson said a trial with AT&T in Arlington, Texas, detected, located and tracked multiple drones using sensing dashboards. A separate demonstration with Erillisverkot in Helsinki used multiple 5G sites to show how network sensing could support public safety and counter-drone operations.

In Poland, Ericsson worked with Asseco and Play on a demonstration combining ISAC technology, Play's mobile network and Asseco's PUSZCZYK acoustic detection system. The companies focused on improving the detection and positioning of low-flying drones near sensitive locations.

items.t: Nokia Tumbles 10% Despite Data Center-Driven Profit Beat; Ericsson Slips
sum: Nokia just beat earnings on surging AI data center demand, yet its stock is cratering while rival Ericsson barely flinches. The reason why reveals something important about where each company is actually making its money.

A profit beat powered by artificial intelligence (AI) data center demand is causing a sharp selloff at one of Europe’s biggest network equipment makers. Nokia (NYSE:NOK | NOK Price Prediction) stock is at $8.34 in early trading, down 10% after the company’s Q3 2026 results topped estimates, a drop that runs counter to the strength of the report.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down 1.37% as investors sell AI names across the board, leaving the decline in Nokia stock far worse than the broad market’s. Tech stocks are generally struggling today, as the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSE ARCA:XLK) is falling 3%. Meanwhile, Ericsson (NASDAQ:ERIC) stock is at $10.29, down 1%, a much softer slide that puts Nokia’s own report at the center of the selling.

Comparable operating profit at Nokia climbed 35% year over year to $679.58 million, beating analyst estimates as demand for networking equipment tied to AI infrastructure accelerated. Revenue at the company reached $5.79 billion, comfortably ahead of the $5.07 billion consensus. The upside came partly from delivering a portion of Nokia’s data center equipment backlog, even as the industry contends with constrained supplies and higher prices for components such as memory chips.

AI & Cloud customers, a group that includes hyperscalers, generated $708.79 million in net sales for Nokia, up 123% at constant currency. Chief Executive Justin Hotard declared, “In AI & Cloud, net sales more than doubled year-over-year and we secured EUR 1.5 billion in new orders.” Nokia’s routing sales also surged, with its IP Networks line jumping 45% on demand from AI & Cloud customers building out data center capacity.

sum: The Finnish telecom equipment maker just posted one of its strongest quarters in years, with artificial intelligence revenue doubling and a €2.8 billion order pipeline that would make any tech CEO envious. Yet the stock is trading nearly 50% below its June peak, and the disconnect between operational momentum and market sentiment has rarely been wider.

Nokia’s comparable operating profit for the second quarter came in at €434 million, handily beating the analyst consensus of €382 million and representing an 18% year-on-year improvement. Revenue rose 8% to €4.82 billion. The standout performer was the AI and cloud division, where sales more than doubled to €446 million — now accounting for 9.3% of total group revenue. Management responded by lifting the full-year operating profit guidance to a range of €2.1 billion to €2.6 billion, up from the previous €2.0 billion to €2.5 billion target.

CEO Justin Hotard has also been busy building for the future. Nokia recently opened an AI Networking Innovation Lab in Sunnyvale, California, where it is collaborating with AMD, Keysight, Lenovo, and Nscale on high-performance networking technologies for AI training and inference. The facility doubles as a validation platform for Nokia’s so-called Validated Designs, testing network architectures under real-world AI workloads.

Despite the strong numbers, Nokia shares have been under heavy pressure. The Nasdaq-listed stock closed Wednesday at $8.41, down 5.82% from the prior day’s close of $8.93. In European trading, the picture was more mixed: after closing at €7.36 on Wednesday, the stock rebounded 5.27% to €7.75 on Thursday. But that bounce comes from deeply oversold territory — the stock is now 50.84% below its 52-week high of €14.97, reached on June 3.

The sell-off was triggered not by the past quarter but by what management sees ahead. Hotard warned that memory chip shortages will persist through 2027, calling the component the single biggest bottleneck across the entire tech industry. That message landed like a lead weight on valuations. The warning was reinforced by rival Ericsson, whose shares tumbled nearly 12% on July 14 after it flagged the same cost inflation in memory chips, dragging the entire telecom equipment sector lower.

Concerns about using Nvidia's GPUs and Intel's CPUs in the RAN are making it easier for Ericsson to justify its work on custom silicon.

To the bemusement of many onlookers, Nvidia has been showering the network hoi polloi with dollars like a farmer scattering grain. It has already plowed $1 billion into Nokia and another $2 billion into Marvell Technology, which makes connectivity chips for the Finnish vendor. The crop for Nvidia would be an even bigger field of graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips it mainly sells to giant data centers for the training of AI's large language models (LLMs). But skepticism about whether those GPUs will take root in the radio access network (RAN) has not abated. The latest forecasts from a respected analyst seem to vindicate the doubts.

Each year, telcos spend about $35 billion on RAN products, according to both Omdia, a Light Reading sister company, and Dell'Oro, another firm that tracks this market. After an initial flurry of spending on 5G network deployment, expenditure is down from a high point of $45 billion in 2022. Neither one of the analyst firms envisages any growth this year. Even worse, though, is Dell'Oro's latest five-year RAN outlook.

Despite much chatter about AI-RAN, the concept promoted by Nvidia, Dell'Oro does not expect it to have a big impact on sales. It will not lead operators to spend more on RAN products than they currently do, according to Stefan Pongratz, a Dell'Oro analyst. Nor will most operators be persuaded to buy GPU-based RAN products for their AI needs, judging by the Dell'Oro forecast. By 2030, what Pongratz calls "GPU RAN" will be a "$1B+ market," said the analyst in his LinkedIn post.

The "+" in that statement clearly gives Dell'Oro a get-out clause should GPU RAN unexpectedly mushroom. Predictions can also be revised upward, as Dell'Oro has recently done. But if the analyst company were today more bullish about GPU RAN, it would naturally have set the floor for revenues at a higher level than $1 billion. As an annual figure, and without growth in the overall RAN market, this would equate to less than 3% of total spending.

Data shared by Ookla shows AT&T's switch from Nokia to a 'single vendor' deal with Ericsson has delivered network improvements.

Ever since AT&T decided to terminate its radio access network (RAN) deal with Nokia in late 2023, the giant US telco has been on the defensive about its commitment to open RAN. Some executives bristled at the suggestion it had opted for a monogamous affair with Ericsson, responsible for about two thirds of its RAN sites at the time of the move. The Swedish company's own newly discovered enthusiasm for open RAN would allow AT&T to pair it with an array of other, lesser-known suppliers and operate a truly multivendor network, the argument went. Yet data shared exclusively with Light Reading by Ookla tells a different story.

Last year, Ericsson's share of AT&T's RAN macro sites rose from 73.84% in the first half (or 1H) to 84.21% in the second, with Nokia still accounting for the rest. As AT&T has ripped out Nokia's old radios and baseband equipment, it has been replacing them with Ericsson's products and leaning even more heavily on the Swedish vendor. The transition has established Ericsson as AT&T's "sole main supplier" and formed part of the telco's shift to a "single vendor strategy," said Ookla in research findings emailed to Light Reading. It has also brought significant improvements in AT&T's network performance.

Indeed, the purpose of Ookla's analysis is not to pass judgment on AT&T's network strategy but rather to measure the performance of competing vendors' RAN products in the three main US mobile networks, the others being Verizon and T-Mobile US. Today, each of those networks features two main product vendors. While Nokia was present at less than 16% of AT&T's RAN sites in the second half of 2025, T-Mobile's network was divided evenly between the Nordic vendors. Verizon, meanwhile, used Ericsson across 60% of its RAN footprint and Samsung for the rest.

Amid the explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI), Nokia has forged a partnership with Nvidia (NVDA +2.77%) that could propel the company far beyond its legacy telecom roots. This strategic pivot raises an interesting question for investors: Is Nokia simply riding a wave of AI hype, or does it offer a rare opportunity to buy a meme stock with genuine substance?

You probably remember Nokia as a popular mobile phone maker from the late 1990s and early 2000s. Its phones were synonymous with reliability and innovation, and powered the first wave of mass-market wireless communication. At its peak, Nokia commanded 40% of the global mobile phone market.

By the mid-2000s, however, the arrival of Apple's iPhone and Alphabet's Google Android ecosystem exposed Nokia's struggles to keep pace with touchscreen smartphones and app-driven software. The company's market share eroded, and in 2014, Nokia sold its mobile division to Microsoft.

While most investors assumed this would be the end of Nokia, the company actually pivoted its focus entirely to telecommunications infrastructure. Today, it builds 5G radio access networks (RAN), optical systems, and IP (internet protocol) routing solutions that power everything from urban broadband to enterprise connectivity.

In October, Nvidia invested $1 billion in Nokia through new stock issued at a price of $6.01 per share. Their collaboration will integrate Nvidia's GPU-powered AI platforms directly into Nokia's RAN portfolio. The goal is to create commercial solutions that embed AI into mobile networks -- enabling smarter, more efficient 5G-advanced and future 6G systems.

Together, Nvidia and Nokia are working on building AI-RAN that optimizes spectrum usage, reduces energy consumption, and handles surging data traffic from expanding AI workloads. The deal positions Nokia as a bridge between traditional telecom environments and the AI economy -- injecting fresh capital and new credibility into its evolution.

Ericsson to modernize SoftBank core network in Japan
sum: STOCKHOLM, March 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ericsson (NASDAQ: ERIC) has signed a multi-year framework agreement with SoftBank Corp. (SoftBank) in Japan to deploy next-generation core network solutions to expand and modernize SoftBank's core network infrastructure and accelerate 5G Standalone (SA) adoption.

The agreement will tap the full scope of Ericsson's Core Networks' portfolio, including the Ericsson dual-mode 5G Core solution running on Ericsson's Cloud Native Infrastructure Solution (CNIS). The deployment will include subscriber data management through Ericsson's User Data Consolidation (UDC) solution, policy control, and cloud-based IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) solutions.

These solutions will enable SoftBank to accelerate its transition to 5G SA while managing existing 4G and 5G services in an integrated manner, improving overall network scalability and reliability. The agreement will also strengthen SoftBank's foundation for 5G Advanced use cases and AI-driven operations across the network.

Hideyuki Tsukuda, Executive Vice President and CTO, SoftBank Corp., says: "Ericsson's advanced cloud-native technologies and automation solutions are an extremely important foundation for achieving the 'fusion of AI and networks' that we are promoting. Through this renewal of our core network, it becomes possible to significantly heighten the autonomy and efficiency of network operations, in addition to accelerating the transition to 5G SA. SoftBank will build a robust and flexible next-generation infrastructure, continuing to provide new value to customers while driving innovation in the telecom industry."

Jawad Mansour, President and Representative Director of Ericsson Japan, says: "We are very pleased that SoftBank, an industry frontrunner in merging AI with telecommunications, has selected our core network and IMS solutions to underpin its further evolution. By combining our technology with global experience, we will support SoftBank's objectives to enhance network performance, improve operational efficiency, and advance the adoption of all forms of automation - contributing to digital transformation that helps address societal challenges in Japan."

Ericsson's CEO said it plans to continue job cuts in the future in order to improve cost efficiency as the vendor faces sluggish growth in one of its core businesses.

"We have reduced the headcount, for example, by 5,000 over the past year," said Ericsson CEO Borje Ekholm on the vendor's Q4 earnings call. "And we expect to continue reducing headcount going forward."
Ekholm highlighted Ericsson's recently announced plans to cut 1,600 jobs in Sweden last week and said the reduction was part of a global effort to improve cost efficiency in its business.
"The underlying demand environment for mobile networks remains actually flattish," the CEO stated. "It is encouraging that we had an organic growth of 6% during Q4."

The reason for this, the CEO said, is that Ericsson has invested in "a number of growth opportunities and growth initiatives" like 5G core, mission-critical networks and enterprises. Wisconsin psychologist shares how to ‘hack’ your emotions
sum: Maybe you’ve had this experience: Something small happens … and it triggers a bigger emotional response than you expected. You’re stuck in traffic and get angry, maybe even yell a little.
Wisconsin psychologist Ryan Martin has been studying emotions for years. And he says there’s good news: We have more control over our emotions than we might think.

Martin, a psychology professor and dean of the College of Arts, Humanities & Social Sciences at the University of Wisconsin-Green Bay, is known as “The Anger Professor.” In his new book, he offers advice on dealing with a wide range of human emotions. It’s called “Emotion Hacks: 50 Ways to Feel Better Fast.”
He told WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” that he wanted to offer practical techniques to help people deal with emotional situations.
“There’s lots of things we can do,” Martin said, “big things and small things that can have a really profound impact on our emotional life.”
Martin breaks an emotional reaction down into a series of steps. “What I want people to understand,” he said, “is that there are different interventions at each and every one of those points.”
Stimulus: “Maybe you get stuck in traffic or maybe you see a scary movie, or maybe you lose something that you care about.”
